content: Salmonella was first identified by Daniel E. Salmon, an American veterinarian, in 1884. He isolated Salmonella choleraesuis from pigs suffering from hog cholera. The association between specific bacterial strains and disease pathogenesis was later established, with genetic mutations implicated in the pathogenicity of Salmonella in subsequent years. Infection with Salmonella begins after ingestion, where the bacteria attach to the intestinal lining using fimbriae or pili. They specifically target specialized epithelial cells, known as M cells, located in the Peyer’s patches of the intestine. The bacteria are internalized through receptor-mediated endocytosis and transported within phagosomes to the lamina propria, where they are released. Once in the lamina propria, Salmonella induces an influx of immune cells—macrophages in typhoidal strains and neutrophils in nontyphoidal strains. The Vi antigen of Salmonella typhi plays a critical role in evading immune responses by preventing antibody-mediated opsonization and complement-mediated lysis. Through cytokine release and mononuclear cell migration, S. typhi spreads via the reticuloendothelial system, primarily targeting the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Within approximately 14 days, the bacteria enter the bloodstream, leading to secondary metastatic infections such as splenic abscesses or endocarditis. In some cases, gallbladder infection results in chronic carriage of S. typhi or S. paratyphi, with continuous shedding of the bacteria in bile and stool. Nontyphoidal Salmonella infections typically cause localized responses, while S. typhi and other virulent strains invade deeper tissues through lymphatics and capillaries, eliciting a robust immune response. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) was first described in 1895 by Dr. Connor in identical twin sisters. In 1921, Dr. Johannes Peutz of Holland identified the link between gastrointestinal polyposis and distinctive skin pigmentation. In 1949, Dr. Harold Jeghers in the United States further established the association between intestinal polyposis, skin pigmentation, and the development of PJS. The term Peutz-Jeghers syndrome was coined by A. Bruwer in 1954. In 1998, mutations in the STK11 (also known as LKB1) gene were implicated in the pathogenesis of PJS. The STK11 protein is crucial for second messenger signal transduction, regulating cellular proliferation, maintaining cell polarity, and responding to low-energy states. In mammalian studies, STK11 inhibits AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and downstream signaling to suppress the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. Dysregulation of the mTOR pathway is a hallmark of PJS. Polyps associated with PJS have a unique histological appearance, characterized by a smooth muscle core that arborizes throughout the polyp. These polyps can only be distinguished from other types through histopathological analysis. PJS is caused by mutations in the STK11 gene, with variable penetrance. The syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1 in 8,300 to 1 in 250,000 individuals, with the most likely prevalence being 1 in 100,000. It affects males and females equally, with symptoms typically appearing between the ages of 10 and 30. The average age of diagnosis is 23 years for males and 26 years for females. The clinical presentation of PJS often begins in the first decade of life with symptoms such as hyperpigmentation, abdominal pain, and rectal bleeding. If untreated, patients are at risk of developing malignancies, including colon, breast, and gastrointestinal cancers. Extraintestinal manifestations include pancreatic, lung, breast, uterine, ovarian, and testicular malignancies. Common complications of PJS include intussusception, gastric outlet obstruction, and extraintestinal polyps. Screening recommendations for PJS, as per the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) and the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), include annual physical examinations, complete blood work to assess for iron deficiency anemia, and endoscopy. Prognosis for PJS varies depending on the extent of disease at diagnosis, but it is generally considered good with appropriate management.
